"Ashford plays the title character in 'Sylvia,' a comedy as predictable as it is indestructible... Shouldn’t we be done with plays like 'Sylvia?' It is antiquated, it is self-congratulatory, it is conservative in both form and content with its focus on the non-problems of upper-middle-class white New Yorkers...
What a joy to see Ashford unleashed.
Daniel Sullivan's spic-and-span production pretty well justifies the Broadway premiere
What makes this production of 'Sylvia' such a treat is the inspired comic chemistry between Broderick and Ashford
As long as we can sit back and laugh at Sylvia’s doggy antics while admiring Ashford’s comic flair, “Sylvia” is harmless fun.
Ms. Parker is funny and touching in equal measure, bringing out both the silliness and the emotional truth
Ashford creates her physically irresistible doggy self in this anthropomorphic lovefest on Broadway.
The production is worth the trip for Ashford's antics alone.
The gimmick of “Sylvia,” which is indeed a comedy — albeit a trifling one — resides in the casting of an actor as Sylvia.

Ashford gives a comic-genius performance, establishing herself as a full-fledged clown star, meaning she’s not only hilarious and eccentric but able to project both qualities, as well as an undertone of pathos, to the back of the house.
And this contributes to the general feeling of weirdness inside the Cort Theatre.

Dog owners in the audience are identifiable by their guffaws over every recognizable mutt mannerism, but there’s enough meat here to sustain a half-hour playlet at best, in an overstretched conceit that runs an interminable two hours-plus.
This truly is one of those must-see performances that will stick with you for some time.

If you are a dog person, you are likely to fall in love with 'Sylvia.' However, Daniel Sullivan's production of A.R. Gurney's 1995 play is so warm and bitingly funny, you'd have to be an absolute Grinch to resist its immense charms.
Anyone looking for a solid example of that most endangered of species, the smart boulevard comedy, should consider adopting 'Sylvia' for an evening's entertainment.
Her facial expressions alone can be worth the price of admission, not to mention the delight of watching her grudgingly roll over, take a shoe in her mouth, or
All in all, Sylvia is a delightfully benign canine-comedy.
Unfortunately, she and Broderick lack chemistry and that is my only problem with an otherwise enjoyable and fun theatrical experience.

Ashford’s consistently hilarious, sometimes touching, always spot-on canine impersonation is the reason to see the first Broadway production of A.R. Gurney’s play about a man who falls in love with a stray dog that he finds in the park, endangering his marriage.
In "Sylvia," which opened in a revival Tuesday night at the Cort Theatre, Annaleigh Ashford portrays the title character, a talking dog, and she is stupendously funny.
This revival proves that some plays are every bit as timeless as man's best friend.
Sylvia is a fanciful but slight dessert sort of a play, so have yourself a satisfying meal before ordering it up.
Fortunately, the verdict rests with the former.
Even the unenlightened -- that is, folks who don't already love dogs -- are bound to lose their hearts.
Much of the play is fun but the march to the end falls rather flat.
I didn’t have an abiding affection for this production, but you could certainly call it puppy love.
It’s just a cute and clever conceit.
All of this gimmickry — some of it written into the play, some of it resulting from Sullivan’s direction — wouldn’t matter if the characters, the dog included, weren’t so dull.
How can anyone not fall in love with Sylvia?
Bottom line: this is a very funny comedy and if you love dogs, you'll love 'Sylvia.'
If dogs could talk, Ashford would be barking up the right tree.
Ashford smartly underplays as much as possible, and it's to her credit that she makes Sylvia funnier and more affecting than it has any right to be.
Ashford is incredibly talented.

Twenty years after its debut at Manhattan Theatre Club, A.R. Gurney’s charming but inconsequential play has finally made it to Broadway. It presents the playwright in a much more favorable light than any of the three Gurney plays that Signature recently mounted.
It's downright shameful when it happens at a $150-a-ticket Broadway play.

cn.t: Critics praise Annaleigh Ashford's delightful performance as the titular dog in Gurney's charming comedy, though some find the 1995 play lightweight. Broderick receives mixed notices, with a few critics finding him disengaged.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
